title: [B1 • Band 5.0] Bài 202: Doggerland: The Submerged Heart of Europe
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 202 (LEVEL B1 • BAND 5.0)

Doggerland: The Submerged Heart of Europe

Paragraph 1. For centuries, fishermen pulling heavy nets across the shallow North Sea returned to port with unusual catches. Mixed among cod and haddock were ancient bones of mammoths, woolly rhinos, and deer, along with bone harpoons. Until the late twentieth century, experts assumed these objects were merely rubbish washed into the ocean by glacial floods. Today, however, modern sea-floor surveys prove that until roughly 8,200 years ago, this area was a dry, fertile landmass linking Britain directly to the Netherlands, Germany, and Denmark. Archaeologists call this lost territory Doggerland.

Paragraph 2. Doggerland was shaped around 18,000 years ago when giant Ice Age glaciers melted, creating wide river valleys, freshwater marshes, lagoons, and oak forests. Excavations show that Mesolithic hunter-gatherers lived comfortably here. Far from facing hunger, local communities enjoyed rich seasonal food supplies including wildfowl, freshwater eels, shellfish, and deer. Objects found on the seabed—such as sharp flint tools, bone needles, and wooden paddles—show that residents built clever equipment for water travel and fishing.

Paragraph 3. Yet Doggerland could not survive rising oceans. Over thousands of years, sea levels climbed steadily at an average pace of nearly one metre per century, flooding low coastal marshes and forcing human groups to move slowly inland toward higher ground. For decades, researchers believed this migration happened peacefully across many generations without sudden danger.

Paragraph 4. Recent ocean studies overturned that calm picture. Around 8,150 years ago, a huge underwater landslide off Norway's coast—the Storegga Slide—moved 3,000 cubic kilometres of mud and triggered an enormous tsunami. A wall of water up to twenty metres tall struck Doggerland's coastal plains, destroying settlements within hours. Any survivors on high hills found their freshwater supplies ruined by salt. Within a few centuries, rising waters covered the remaining hills and separated Britain from mainland Europe.

Paragraph 5. Mapping a drowned country thirty metres beneath shifting mud is extremely hard. Because normal land digging is useless underwater, geophysicist Dr. Vincent Gaffney reused seismic data originally gathered by oil and gas firms searching for North Sea energy reserves. By processing these records with advanced software, his team digitally removed the seabed mud and mapped over 45,000 square kilometres of ancient rivers, lakes, and hills.

groups.title: Questions 6–10
groups.instructions: Do the following statements agree with the information in the passage? Write TRUE, FALSE, or NOT GIVEN.

steps: Đoạn 1: "...washed into the ocean by glacial floods."
Đoạn 1: "...linking Britain directly to the Netherlands, Germany, and Denmark."
Đoạn 2: "...wooden paddles—show that residents built clever equipment for water travel..."
Đoạn 4: "...found their freshwater supplies ruined by salt."
Đoạn 5: "...reused seismic data originally gathered by oil and gas firms..."

q6.text: Until the late 1900s, experts realised Doggerland had once been a populated landmass.

steps: Đoạn 1: Trước cuối thế kỷ 20, chuyên gia tưởng đó chỉ là rác trôi do lũ băng, chưa biết đó là vùng đất màu mỡ.

q7.text: Mesolithic communities in Doggerland suffered from constant food shortages.

steps: Đoạn 2: "Far from facing hunger, local communities enjoyed rich seasonal food supplies..."

q8.text: Sea levels rose at the exact same speed in every single month of the year.

steps: Đoạn 3: Bài chỉ nêu tốc độ trung bình gần 1 mét mỗi thế kỷ, không nói tốc độ giống hệt nhau từng tháng trong năm.

q9.text: The Storegga Slide tsunami destroyed settlements very quickly.

q10.text: Oil and gas firms originally collected North Sea data to help archaeologists.

steps: Đoạn 5: Các công ty thu thập dữ liệu để tìm trữ lượng năng lượng (dầu khí), không phải giúp khảo cổ.
